# RateKit — Full Reference (llms-full.txt)

> Complete formulas, worked examples and FAQ text for every RateKit calculator, in one file, for AI agents and language models that want full context without crawling 18 separate pages. Short directory: llms.txt. Machine-readable API spec: openapi.json.

## Freelance Rate Calculator
URL: https://ratekit.org/freelance-rate
Calculate your minimum freelance hourly rate based on income goals, expenses, tax rate, and working schedule. Free, instant, no signup.

Formula:
Hourly rate = (Target income + Annual expenses) / (1 - Tax rate) / Billable hours per year
Billable hours = Working weeks x Hours per week x Billable %

FAQ:
Q: What is a good hourly rate for a freelancer?
A: It depends on your market and skill, but your floor is the break-even rate from this calculator: target income plus expenses and taxes, divided by realistic billable hours. Price above that floor based on the value you deliver.
Q: How many billable hours does a freelancer have per year?
A: Typically 1,000-1,400. A 40-hour week over 46 weeks is 1,840 hours, but only 50-70% of that is usually billable.
Q: Should I charge hourly or per project?
A: Use the hourly rate as your internal floor, then quote per project or per day where you can. Clients compare outcomes, and fixed prices reward you for working efficiently.

---

## Salary ↔ Hourly Calculator
URL: https://ratekit.org/salary-hourly
Convert annual salary to hourly rate or hourly rate to annual salary. Accounts for work hours, paid time off, and holidays. Free salary converter.

Formula:
Hourly rate = Annual salary / (Hours per week x Weeks per year)
Standard: Annual salary / 2,080
Monthly pay = Annual salary / 12

FAQ:
Q: How many working hours are in a year?
A: 2,080 for a standard 40-hour week over 52 weeks. After holidays and vacation, most people actually work 1,900-2,000 hours.
Q: How much is $30 an hour per year?
A: About $62,400 per year at 2,080 hours, before taxes.
Q: How do I compare a salary with a freelance rate?
A: Freelancers need a much higher hourly rate than the salary equivalent to cover unpaid hours, self-employment tax, benefits and expenses, often 1.5-2 times the salaried hourly rate.

---

## 1099 vs W2 Calculator
URL: https://ratekit.org/1099-vs-w2
Compare 1099 contractor vs W2 employee compensation. Calculate take-home pay, taxes, and benefits to decide which is better for you. Free 2026 calculator.

Formula:
Contractor net = 1099 income - SE tax - Income tax - Benefits you buy - Business expenses
Employee net = Salary - Employee FICA (7.65%) - Income tax, plus the value of employer benefits

FAQ:
Q: Is it better to be 1099 or W-2?
A: W-2 gives stability, employer-paid payroll tax and benefits. 1099 gives flexibility and business deductions, but you pay the full 15.3% SE tax. Compare total net income, not headline pay.
Q: How much more should a 1099 contractor charge?
A: Typically 25-40% more than the equivalent W-2 hourly wage to cover SE tax, benefits, unpaid time off and business costs.
Q: Can 1099 contractors deduct expenses?
A: Yes. Ordinary and necessary business expenses reduce taxable profit, and half of SE tax is deductible. Some may also qualify for the QBI deduction.

## Stripe & PayPal Fee Calculator
URL: https://ratekit.org/stripe-fee
Calculate exact Stripe and PayPal fees. Find out how much to charge your client to receive your desired amount after processing fees. Free, instant.

Formula:
Fee = Amount x Percentage + Fixed fee
You receive = Amount - Fee
To receive X, charge = (X + Fixed fee) / (1 - Percentage)

FAQ:
Q: How much does Stripe charge per transaction?',     a: "Standard US pricing is 2.9% + $0.30 per successful card charge. International cards and currency conversion add extra fees. Check Stripe's pricing page for your country." },   { q: 'How do I pass the Stripe fee to the customer?
A: Gross up the price: charge (desired amount + fixed fee) / (1 - percentage). Surcharging rules differ by country and card network, so check local rules first.
Q: Is Stripe or PayPal cheaper?
A: At standard US rates Stripe (2.9% + $0.30) is cheaper than PayPal checkout (3.49% + $0.49) for most amounts, but negotiated and regional pricing can change that.

## VAT & GST Calculator
URL: https://ratekit.org/vat-calculator
Add or remove VAT and GST from any price. Supports all countries and custom rates. Free VAT calculator for invoicing and business.

Formula:
Add VAT: Gross = Net x (1 + Rate)
Remove VAT: Net = Gross / (1 + Rate)
VAT amount = Gross - Net

FAQ:
Q: How do I calculate VAT from a gross amount?
A: Divide the gross amount by (1 + VAT rate) to get the net price; the difference is the VAT. For 20% VAT: 120 / 1.2 = 100 net and 20 VAT.
Q: What is the difference between VAT and GST?
A: Both are value-added consumption taxes; the name depends on the country (VAT in the EU and UK, GST in Australia, Canada, India, Singapore). The calculation is the same.

## Invoice Generator
URL: https://ratekit.org/invoice-generator
Create professional invoices instantly. Download as PDF. Free invoice generator for freelancers and small businesses. No signup required.

Formula:
Line total = Quantity x Unit price
Subtotal = Sum of line totals
Total due = Subtotal - Discount + Tax

FAQ:
Q: What are standard invoice payment terms?
A: Net 30 (payment within 30 days) is the most common; freelancers increasingly use Net 7 or Net 15. A clear due date reduces late payments.
Q: Do I need to add VAT to my invoice?
A: Only if you are VAT or GST registered, or otherwise required to charge it. Show the rate and tax amount separately.
Q: Is this invoice generator free?
A: Yes. It is free and requires no signup.

---

## Self-Employment Tax Calculator
URL: https://ratekit.org/self-employment-tax
Calculate US self-employment tax (15.3%), quarterly estimated payments, and how much to set aside from each paycheck. Free SE tax calculator for freelancers.

Formula:
SE earnings = Net profit x 92.35%
SE tax = SE earnings x 12.4% (Social Security, up to the annual wage base) + SE earnings x 2.9% (Medicare)
Income-tax deduction = SE tax / 2

FAQ:
Q: What is the self-employment tax rate?
A: 15.3%: 12.4% Social Security plus 2.9% Medicare, applied to 92.35% of net earnings. Social Security applies only up to the annual wage base; an additional 0.9% Medicare tax applies above $200,000 for single filers.
Q: Do I need to pay quarterly estimated taxes?
A: Generally yes, if you expect to owe $1,000 or more for the year. Payments are due in April, June, September and January.
Q: How much should I set aside for taxes as a freelancer?
A: A common rule of thumb is 25-30% of net profit to cover SE tax and federal income tax, plus state tax where applicable.

---

## Form 2555 — Foreign Earned Income Exclusion
URL: https://ratekit.org/form-2555
Calculate your IRS Form 2555 Foreign Earned Income Exclusion (FEIE) for 2026. Find out how much US expats can exclude from taxable income. Free calculator.

Formula:
Excluded income = min(Foreign earned income, Annual FEIE limit x Qualifying days / Days in year)
Physical presence test: 330 full days outside the US in a 12-month period

FAQ:
Q: Who can use Form 2555?
A: US citizens and resident aliens with foreign earned income and a tax home abroad who meet either the bona fide residence test or the physical presence test.
Q: Does the FEIE remove self-employment tax?
A: No. The exclusion applies to income tax only; self-employed expats still owe US self-employment tax unless a totalization agreement applies.
Q: FEIE or Foreign Tax Credit: which is better?
A: In low-tax countries the FEIE usually saves more; in high-tax countries the Foreign Tax Credit (Form 1116) is often better. Some expats combine both.

---

## Deal Coach
URL: https://ratekit.org/deal-coach
AI-powered negotiation coach for freelancers and founders. Get structured arguments for rate negotiation and equity/SAFE discussions. Free tool by RateKit.

Formula:
Prepare: BATNA (best alternative) -> Walk-away point -> Target -> Opening offer
ZOPA = overlap between your walk-away point and theirs

FAQ:
Q: What is BATNA?
A: Best Alternative To a Negotiated Agreement: what you will do if this deal fails. A strong BATNA gives you leverage and sets your walk-away point.
Q: Should I make the first offer?
A: Often yes, if you have done your research: the first number anchors the negotiation. Open ambitiously but justifiably.
Q: How do I negotiate without lowering my price?
A: Trade variables instead of discounts: scope, timeline, payment terms, volume or contract length.

---

## ROI Calculator
URL: https://ratekit.org/roi-calculator
Calculate Return on Investment (ROI), annualized ROI, and payback period. Free ROI calculator for marketing, business investments, and projects.

Formula:
ROI = (Gain from investment - Cost of investment) / Cost of investment x 100%
Annualized ROI = (1 + ROI)^(1 / Years) - 1

FAQ:
Q: What is a good ROI?
A: It depends on risk and time. Many businesses target marketing ROI above 100% (earning $2 for every $1 spent), while long-term investments are often compared to a 7-10% annual market return.
Q: What is the difference between ROI and ROAS?
A: ROAS divides revenue by ad spend; ROI subtracts all costs and divides profit by investment. A campaign can have a high ROAS and still a negative ROI if margins are thin.
Q: Should I use revenue or profit in the ROI formula?
A: Use profit (gain minus all related costs). Using revenue overstates ROI.

---

## Profit Margin Calculator
URL: https://ratekit.org/profit-margin
Calculate gross profit margin, net profit margin, and markup. Free profit margin calculator for e-commerce, retail, and business pricing.

Formula:
Gross margin = (Price - Cost) / Price x 100%
Markup = (Price - Cost) / Cost x 100%
Price for a target margin = Cost / (1 - Margin)

FAQ:
Q: What is the difference between margin and markup?
A: Margin is profit divided by price; markup is profit divided by cost. The same $40 profit on a $100 price is a 40% margin but a 66.7% markup.
Q: What is a good profit margin for a small business?
A: It varies by industry: services and software often run 20-40% or more, retail and restaurants 3-10% net. Compare with businesses in your sector.

---

## Break-even Calculator
URL: https://ratekit.org/break-even
Calculate your break-even point in units and revenue. Find out how many sales you need to cover fixed and variable costs. Free tool for businesses and startups.

Formula:
Contribution margin per unit = Price - Variable cost per unit
Break-even units = Fixed costs / Contribution margin per unit
Break-even revenue = Break-even units x Price

FAQ:
Q: What costs are fixed and which are variable?',     a: "Fixed costs don't change with sales volume (rent, salaries, software). Variable costs grow with each unit sold (materials, payment fees, shipping, commissions)." },   { q: 'How can I lower my break-even point?
A: Raise prices, cut variable costs per unit, or reduce fixed costs. Raising price usually has the biggest effect because it goes straight to contribution margin.
Q: What is the margin of safety?
A: How far current sales are above break-even: (Actual sales - Break-even sales) / Actual sales. It shows how much sales can drop before you start losing money.

---

## Business Loan & APR Calculator
URL: https://ratekit.org/loan-calculator
Calculate monthly payments, total interest, and true APR for business loans. Compare loan options side by side. Free loan calculator for entrepreneurs.

Formula:
Monthly payment = P x r / (1 - (1 + r)^(-n))
P = loan amount, r = annual rate / 12, n = number of monthly payments
Total interest = Payment x n - P

FAQ:
Q: What is the difference between interest rate and APR?
A: The interest rate is the cost of borrowing the principal; APR also includes origination and other fees, expressed as a yearly rate. Compare loans by APR.
Q: How can I lower my monthly loan payment?
A: Choose a longer term, negotiate a lower rate, or borrow less. A longer term lowers payments but increases total interest paid.
Q: What is a factor rate?
A: Some short-term lenders quote a factor (for example 1.2) instead of an interest rate: you repay 1.2 times the amount borrowed. Converted to APR, factor-rate loans are often very expensive.

---

## Profit & Loss Statement
URL: https://ratekit.org/pl-statement
Build your Profit & Loss statement online. Auto-calculates gross profit, EBITDA, and net profit. Free P&L tool for businesses and startups.

Formula:
Gross profit = Revenue - Cost of goods sold (COGS)
Operating profit (EBIT) = Gross profit - Operating expenses
Net profit = Operating profit - Interest - Taxes

FAQ:
Q: What is the difference between a P&L and a cash flow statement?
A: The P&L shows profitability when revenue is earned and costs are incurred; the cash flow statement shows when cash actually moves. A profitable business can still run out of cash.
Q: What goes into COGS?
A: Direct costs of delivering your product or service: materials, production, direct labor, hosting for SaaS, and payment processing tied to sales.
Q: How often should I prepare a P&L?
A: Monthly for management decisions, quarterly for investors and lenders, and annually for taxes.

---

## Budget & Cash Flow Calculator
URL: https://ratekit.org/budget-calculator
Free monthly budget calculator with 12-month cash flow forecast and runway. See profit/loss, margin, and best/worst-case revenue scenarios instantly.

Formula:
Total Costs = Fixed Costs + (Revenue × Variable Cost %)
Profit/Loss = Revenue − Total Costs
Runway (months) = Starting Cash ÷ |Profit/Loss|   (only when Profit/Loss is negative)

FAQ:
Q: How is runway different from burn rate?
A: Burn rate is how much cash you lose per month. Runway is how many months you can survive at that burn rate — cash on hand divided by the monthly loss.
Q: Should I include my own salary in fixed costs?',     a: "Yes. Founder pay is a real cash cost even if you plan to defer it — exclude it and your budget will understate how much cash you actually need." },   { q: 'What counts as a variable cost?
A: Costs that scale with revenue or volume: payment processing fees, materials, shipping, sales commissions. If a cost stays the same whether you sell $0 or $100k, it is fixed, not variable.
Q: How often should I update my budget?',     a: "Monthly, right after you close the books for the previous month. Swap projected numbers for actuals so the forecast stays grounded instead of drifting from your original assumptions." },   { q: 'What if my profit is positive — do I still have a runway number?
A: No — runway only applies when you are losing money. A positive monthly profit means your cash balance grows every month, so there is no countdown to calculate.

---

## SAFE Note Equity Calculator
URL: https://ratekit.org/safe-calculator
Calculate your SAFE note conversion, ownership percentage, and dilution. Supports valuation cap, discount rate. Free tool for founders and investors.

Formula:
Ownership (post-money SAFE) = Investment / Post-money valuation cap
Conversion price = lower of (Cap price, Round price x (1 - Discount))

FAQ:
Q: What is the difference between pre-money and post-money SAFEs?',     a: "In a post-money SAFE the cap includes all SAFE money, so each investor's ownership is fixed and founders absorb dilution from later SAFEs. In older pre-money SAFEs, SAFE holders dilute each other." },   { q: 'How much dilution should founders expect from SAFEs?
A: Add up investment / post-money cap for every SAFE. Raising $1M in SAFEs at a $10M post-money cap means about 10% dilution before the priced round.
Q: Does a SAFE have a discount?
A: Some do. Common forms offer a valuation cap, a discount (often 10-25%), both, or neither (MFN only). The investor gets whichever gives the lower conversion price.

## Burn Rate & Runway Calculator
URL: https://ratekit.org/burn-rate
Calculate your startup's gross and net burn rate, cash runway in months, and zero-cash date. Free tool for founders and CFOs.

Formula:
Gross burn = Total monthly operating expenses
Net burn = Monthly expenses - Monthly revenue
Runway (months) = Cash in bank / Net burn

FAQ:
Q: What is the difference between gross and net burn?
A: Gross burn is total monthly spending. Net burn subtracts revenue and shows how fast your cash balance actually falls.
Q: How much runway should a startup have?
A: Commonly 18-24 months after a raise. Start fundraising with at least 6-9 months left, since rounds often take 3-6 months to close.
Q: How can I extend runway?
A: Cut or delay the biggest expense lines (usually hiring), increase revenue or collections, renegotiate contracts, or raise bridge funding.

---

## LTV : CAC Calculator
URL: https://ratekit.org/ltv-cac
Calculate Customer Lifetime Value (LTV) and Customer Acquisition Cost (CAC). Find out if your unit economics are healthy. Free tool for SaaS and startups.

Formula:
LTV = Monthly revenue per customer x Gross margin / Monthly churn rate
CAC = Sales and marketing spend / New customers acquired
CAC payback (months) = CAC / (Monthly revenue per customer x Gross margin)

FAQ:
Q: What is a good LTV to CAC ratio?
A: About 3:1 is the common benchmark. Below 1:1 you lose money on each customer; far above 5:1 may mean you are under-investing in growth.
Q: What is a good CAC payback period?
A: For SaaS, under 12 months is healthy and under 6 months is excellent.
Q: Should LTV use revenue or gross margin?
A: Gross margin. Revenue-based LTV overstates value because it ignores the cost of serving the customer.

---

## Mental Math Challenge
URL: https://ratekit.org/math-quiz
A free 60-second mental math quiz for founders and freelancers: margins, ROI, discounts, break-even. No calculator allowed — keep your brain sharp.

FAQ:
Q: Is this quiz free?
A: Yes — completely free, no signup, no data stored. Your score only lives in your browser tab.
Q: How is the score calculated?
A: Each correct answer is worth 10 points. Answer all 10 questions correctly for a 20-point perfect-round bonus. Running out of time on a question counts as a miss.
Q: Does practicing mental math actually help in business?
A: Yes. Being able to sanity-check a margin, a discount, or a runway estimate in your head — even roughly — helps you catch bad numbers before you act on them. It will not replace a real calculator for anything that matters, but it builds number intuition.
Q: I got a low score — where should I practice for real?
A: Every question in this quiz is based on a real RateKit calculator. Check the related tools below to work through the actual math slowly, with formulas shown.

# Glossary (full text)

> Plain-English definitions for business/finance terms used across RateKit. Short directory: /glossary.

## ROI (Return on Investment)
URL: https://ratekit.org/glossary/roi
ROI measures how much profit an investment generated relative to its cost, expressed as a percentage.

Formula: ROI = (Net Profit / Cost of Investment) × 100

Return on Investment (ROI) is the most widely used metric for judging whether money spent on a campaign, a piece of equipment, or a project paid off. It strips away the dollar amounts and expresses the result as a single percentage, which makes it easy to compare completely different kinds of spending — a $500 ad campaign and a $50,000 piece of machinery can both be scored on the same scale.

ROI has one well-known blind spot: it ignores time. A 50% ROI earned in one month is a very different result from a 50% ROI earned over five years, which is why marketers and investors often also look at annualized ROI — the same return normalized to a 12-month period — when comparing investments with different holding periods.

ROI also says nothing about risk. A high-ROI investment that could just as easily have lost money is not automatically better than a lower, more reliable return. Use ROI to compare similar bets, not to replace judgment about how likely each outcome actually was.

---

## Break-Even Point
URL: https://ratekit.org/glossary/break-even-point
The break-even point is the sales volume — in units or revenue — at which total revenue equals total costs, so profit is exactly zero.

Formula: Break-even units = Fixed Costs / (Price − Variable Cost per unit)

Every business has costs that don't move with sales volume — rent, salaries, software subscriptions — and costs that scale with each unit sold, like materials or payment processing fees. The break-even point is the exact number of units (or the exact revenue figure) where the money coming in from sales finally covers both kinds of costs completely, with nothing left over and nothing short.

Below the break-even point, every sale still loses the business money overall, even if each individual unit is sold at a profit on paper — because the fixed costs haven't been paid off yet. Above it, every additional unit sold drops straight to the bottom line as profit, since the fixed costs are already covered.

Break-even analysis is one of the first things a new business or new product line should calculate, because it turns "will this work?" into a concrete, falsifiable number: a specific sales target to hit, rather than a vague hope.

---

## Contribution Margin
URL: https://ratekit.org/glossary/contribution-margin
Contribution margin is the revenue left from one unit of sale after subtracting only the variable costs tied to that unit — the amount it \"contributes\" toward covering fixed costs and profit.

Formula: Contribution Margin = Price − Variable Cost per Unit

Contribution margin answers a narrower question than profit margin: not "is this unit profitable after everything?" but "how much does each unit sold help pay down the bills that don't change with volume?" It's calculated per unit (or as a ratio, contribution margin ÷ price) and deliberately excludes fixed costs like rent or salaries.

This makes it the key input to break-even analysis — fixed costs divided by contribution margin tells you exactly how many units you need to sell before fixed costs are covered and every further sale is pure profit. A healthy contribution margin ratio also tells you how much cushion you have to absorb a price cut or a cost increase without losing money on each sale.

---

## Markup vs. Margin
URL: https://ratekit.org/glossary/markup-vs-margin
Markup is profit expressed as a percentage of cost; margin is the same profit expressed as a percentage of selling price. They always give different numbers for the same sale.

Markup and margin are the single most commonly confused pair of numbers in pricing, because they describe the exact same dollar amount of profit from two different starting points. If something costs you $60 and you sell it for $100, your profit is $40. As a markup (profit ÷ cost), that's 66.7%. As a margin (profit ÷ selling price), that's 40%. Both are correct; they're just answering different questions.

The practical risk is using a markup percentage where a margin percentage was intended, or vice versa — a common mistake is setting a "50% margin" by simply adding 50% to cost, which actually produces only a 33.3% margin, not 50%. If you want a true 50% margin, you need a 100% markup on cost.

As a rule of thumb: markup is always a larger number than margin for the same sale, because cost is always lower than selling price, so the same profit dollars make up a bigger share of the smaller number.

---

## Burn Rate
URL: https://ratekit.org/glossary/burn-rate
Burn rate is how much cash a company spends per month, usually split into gross burn (total spending) and net burn (spending minus revenue).

Burn rate is the startup-world term for a company's monthly cash outflow. Gross burn is simply total monthly operating expenses — payroll, rent, software, everything. Net burn subtracts whatever revenue came in that month, and is the number that actually determines how fast the bank balance is falling.

A profitable, revenue-generating company can have a high gross burn but zero or negative net burn, meaning cash is actually growing. A pre-revenue startup's gross and net burn are usually identical, since there's no revenue to offset spending.

Investors watch burn rate closely because, combined with cash in the bank, it determines runway — how many months the company can operate before running out of money. A sudden, unexplained jump in burn rate is one of the first warning signs investors look for in board updates.

---

## Startup Runway
URL: https://ratekit.org/glossary/runway
Runway is how many months a company can keep operating at its current burn rate before its cash balance hits zero.

Formula: Runway (months) = Cash in Bank / Net Burn Rate

Runway answers the single most urgent question for an early-stage company: how much time is left before the money runs out? It's calculated by dividing current cash on hand by the net monthly burn rate, assuming spending and revenue stay roughly constant.

The common advice is to start fundraising with at least 6-9 months of runway remaining, not when the bank account is nearly empty — because a fundraise typically takes 3-6 months from first pitch to money in the bank, and negotiating from a position of scarcity produces worse terms. Investors generally like to see 18-24 months of runway right after a round closes.

Runway is a moving target, not a fixed number: any change in hiring, spend, or revenue growth immediately shifts it, which is why most founders recalculate it monthly rather than treating it as a one-time estimate.

---

## Customer Acquisition Cost (CAC)
URL: https://ratekit.org/glossary/cac
CAC is the total sales and marketing cost to acquire one new customer, calculated by dividing total spend by the number of customers acquired.

Formula: CAC = Total Sales & Marketing Spend / New Customers Acquired

Customer Acquisition Cost is exactly what it sounds like: how much, on average, it costs a business to turn a stranger into a paying customer. It's calculated over a period — usually a month or a quarter — by dividing everything spent on sales and marketing in that period by the number of new customers that period produced.

CAC on its own doesn't tell you whether a business is healthy; it only becomes meaningful next to Customer Lifetime Value (LTV). A $500 CAC is a disaster for a product that generates $100 of lifetime profit per customer, and a bargain for one that generates $5,000. That comparison is exactly what the LTV:CAC ratio measures.

CAC tends to rise as a channel matures and the cheapest, most obvious customers have already been captured — a rising CAC over time, even with flat ad spend, is often a sign that a growth channel is saturating.

---

## Customer Lifetime Value (LTV)
URL: https://ratekit.org/glossary/ltv
LTV is the total gross profit a business expects to earn from a customer over the entire time they remain a customer.

Formula: LTV = (Monthly Revenue per Customer × Gross Margin) / Monthly Churn Rate

Customer Lifetime Value estimates the total profit — not revenue — a typical customer is worth over their whole relationship with a business, from first purchase to the day they leave. For subscription businesses, it's usually calculated from monthly revenue per customer, gross margin, and the monthly churn rate, since 1 ÷ churn rate gives the average customer lifespan in months.

A common mistake is calculating LTV from revenue instead of gross profit, which overstates the number by ignoring the cost of actually serving the customer — hosting, support, payment processing, cost of goods. A correct LTV is always a profit figure, since it's meant to be compared against CAC, which is also a cost.

Because churn rate sits in the denominator, LTV is extremely sensitive to small changes in retention — cutting monthly churn in half roughly doubles LTV, which is why reducing churn is usually a higher-leverage lever than increasing acquisition spend.

---

## LTV:CAC Ratio
URL: https://ratekit.org/glossary/ltv-cac-ratio
The LTV:CAC ratio compares what a customer is worth (LTV) to what it costs to acquire them (CAC); 3:1 is the widely cited healthy benchmark for SaaS businesses.

The LTV:CAC ratio is the single number most often used to judge whether a company's growth is sustainable. Below 1:1, the business loses money on every customer it acquires, no matter how much revenue shows up on the top line. Between 1:1 and 3:1 is considered marginal — the unit economics work, but with little room for error.

3:1 to 5:1 is generally treated as the healthy range: customers generate meaningfully more value than they cost to acquire, while the business is still spending enough on growth to keep winning new customers. A ratio well above 5:1 can actually be a yellow flag rather than purely good news — it often means a company is being too conservative with growth spending.

The ratio should always be read alongside CAC payback period (how many months it takes to recover the acquisition cost), since a business can have excellent long-term unit economics and still run out of cash waiting for that payback to happen.

---

## SAFE Note
URL: https://ratekit.org/glossary/safe-note
A SAFE (Simple Agreement for Future Equity) is a startup fundraising instrument where an investor gives money now in exchange for equity at a future priced round, instead of receiving shares immediately.

A SAFE, created by Y Combinator in 2013, lets early-stage startups raise money without first agreeing on a company valuation — a notoriously hard thing to price accurately pre-revenue. The investor hands over cash now; in exchange, they get the right to convert that investment into equity later, when the company raises a priced round.

Most SAFEs include a valuation cap (a ceiling on the valuation used to calculate the investor's conversion price), a discount (a percentage off the price other investors pay in that future round), or both. The investor converts at whichever term gives them the better, lower price.

Since 2018, Y Combinator's standard SAFE is "post-money" — the valuation cap already accounts for all other SAFEs and the option pool, meaning each SAFE's ownership percentage is fixed and known at signing. Earlier "pre-money" SAFEs could dilute each other in ways that were hard to predict until the priced round actually happened.

---

## Equity Dilution
URL: https://ratekit.org/glossary/equity-dilution
Dilution is the reduction in an existing shareholder's ownership percentage that happens when a company issues new shares to new investors.

Every time a company raises money by selling new shares — through a SAFE, a priced funding round, or a new employee stock option grant — the total number of shares outstanding goes up. Since each existing shareholder still owns the same number of shares as before, but the total pie has more slices, their percentage ownership goes down. That's dilution.

Dilution isn't inherently bad: a smaller slice of a much bigger pie is usually a good trade for founders and early investors. The problem is uncontrolled or poorly understood dilution — stacking SAFEs at low caps, oversized option pools, or down rounds — which can leave founders with far less of the company than they expected by the time it's acquired or goes public.

Founders typically track a "cap table" that shows exactly who owns what percentage after every round, so dilution from each new raise can be modeled and negotiated before it happens, not discovered afterward.

---

## VAT / GST (Value Added Tax)
URL: https://ratekit.org/glossary/vat-gst
VAT (or GST) is a consumption tax added at each stage of production and collected by the seller, ultimately paid by the end consumer.

VAT (used in the EU, UK, and most of the world) and GST (used in countries like Australia, Canada, and India) are functionally the same kind of tax under different names: a percentage added to the price of most goods and services, collected by the business selling them, and remitted to the government. Unlike US sales tax, VAT/GST is typically charged and reclaimed at every stage of a supply chain, with only the end consumer ultimately bearing the cost.

For a business, the practical complexity is usually around invoicing correctly — showing tax separately, applying the right rate for the right country and product category — and reclaiming VAT paid on business purchases against VAT collected on sales; the difference is what actually gets paid to the tax authority.

Rates vary enormously by country and even by product category within a country (many countries apply a reduced rate to food, books, or children's goods), which is why cross-border sellers usually need a tool that tracks current rates by jurisdiction rather than memorizing a single number.

---

## Self-Employment Tax
URL: https://ratekit.org/glossary/self-employment-tax
US self-employment tax is a 15.3% tax covering Social Security and Medicare, paid by freelancers and independent contractors in place of the payroll taxes an employer would normally split with an employee.

Formula: SE Tax = Net Earnings × 92.35% × 15.3% (12.4% Social Security + 2.9% Medicare)

When you work as a W-2 employee, your employer pays half of your Social Security and Medicare taxes (7.65%) and withholds the other half from your paycheck. When you're self-employed, there's no employer to split that cost, so you pay both halves yourself: 15.3% total, applied to 92.35% of your net self-employment earnings.

This is on top of, not instead of, regular federal and state income tax — which is why many new freelancers are caught off guard the first time they see their full tax bill. A common rule of thumb is to set aside 25-30% of net profit for taxes throughout the year, since the US tax system expects self-employed people to pay estimated taxes quarterly.

Half of the self-employment tax paid is deductible when calculating adjusted gross income, which softens the blow slightly, but it's still the single biggest tax-planning surprise for people transitioning from a salaried job to self-employment.

---

## FEIE (Foreign Earned Income Exclusion)
URL: https://ratekit.org/glossary/feie
The FEIE lets qualifying US citizens living abroad exclude a set amount of foreign-earned income from US federal income tax each year.

The United States taxes its citizens on worldwide income no matter where they live — almost uniquely among countries. The Foreign Earned Income Exclusion, claimed via IRS Form 2555, is the main relief valve for Americans living and working abroad: it lets them exclude a set dollar amount of foreign wages or self-employment income from US income tax each year.

To qualify, you need a tax home in a foreign country and need to pass either the Bona Fide Residence Test (established residency abroad for a full tax year) or the Physical Presence Test (at least 330 full days outside the US in any 12-month period). If you qualify for only part of the year, the exclusion limit is prorated.

The FEIE only reduces income tax — it does not reduce US self-employment tax, which self-employed expats still owe in full unless a specific totalization agreement applies. Expats in high-tax countries sometimes do better with the Foreign Tax Credit instead of, or alongside, the FEIE.

---

## APR (Annual Percentage Rate)
URL: https://ratekit.org/glossary/apr
APR is the yearly cost of borrowing money, expressed as a percentage, including both the interest rate and most upfront fees — making it the right number for comparing loans with different fee structures.

The interest rate on a loan tells you how much interest accrues on the outstanding balance. APR goes further: it folds in origination fees and other upfront charges, spreading them across the loan term to produce a single annualized percentage that represents the loan's true cost.

Two loans with the identical interest rate can have very different APRs if one charges a 3% origination fee and the other charges none — APR is what makes that difference visible and comparable, rather than requiring you to do the fee math yourself for every offer.

Short-term lenders sometimes quote a "factor rate" instead of an interest rate (e.g., repay 1.2× what you borrowed). Factor rates look deceptively small because they aren't annualized — converted to APR, many factor-rate loans turn out to carry effective annual rates well over 40-50%.

---

## Loan Amortization
URL: https://ratekit.org/glossary/amortization
Amortization is the process of paying off a loan through equal periodic payments, where each payment covers that period's interest plus a growing share of the principal.

An amortizing loan — most mortgages, auto loans, and standard business term loans — is structured so every payment is the same dollar amount for the life of the loan, but the mix inside each payment changes over time. Early payments are mostly interest, because the outstanding balance is still large; later payments are mostly principal, because the balance has shrunk.

An amortization schedule is a table showing, payment by payment, exactly how much went to interest versus principal, and what the remaining balance is afterward. It's useful for understanding total interest cost, and for deciding whether an extra principal payment is worth making — it almost always is, early in the loan, when the interest share is highest.

The monthly payment itself is calculated once, up front, from the loan amount, interest rate, and term — it doesn't need to be recalculated each month unless the rate changes, as with an adjustable-rate loan.

---

## EBITDA
URL: https://ratekit.org/glossary/ebitda
EBITDA (Earnings Before Interest, Taxes, Depreciation, and Amortization) is a measure of a company's core operating profitability, stripped of financing and accounting decisions.

EBITDA starts from net profit and adds back interest expense, taxes, depreciation, and amortization — four items that have nothing to do with how well the underlying business operates, and everything to do with how it's financed, where it's taxed, and how its accountants depreciate assets on paper. What's left is a rough proxy for the cash-generating power of the core business.

Investors and acquirers favor EBITDA because it allows an apples-to-apples comparison between companies with very different capital structures or tax situations — a company funded entirely by equity and one funded heavily by debt can look very different on net profit alone, purely because of interest expense.

EBITDA is not the same as cash flow and has been criticized for making leveraged or capital-intensive businesses look healthier than they are, since it ignores both debt payments and ongoing capital expenditure. It's a useful comparison metric, not a substitute for looking at actual cash in the bank.

---

## Billable vs. Non-Billable Hours
URL: https://ratekit.org/glossary/billable-hours
Billable hours are time spent on work a client directly pays for; non-billable hours cover everything else a freelancer or agency does to keep the business running.

Billable hours are the only hours that generate revenue directly — writing the code, designing the asset, running the consultation the client is actually paying for. Non-billable hours cover everything that supports that work but isn't itself billed: sending invoices, finding new clients, revising proposals, bookkeeping, and ordinary business admin.

The gap between the two is the single biggest reason a freelance hourly rate needs to be much higher than an equivalent employee's hourly wage. A freelancer who wants to take home $75,000 a year can't just divide that by 2,080 working hours, because a large share of those hours — often 20-30% — will be non-billable. The target income has to be divided by billable hours only.

Agencies and consultancies track a "utilization rate" (billable hours ÷ total hours available) precisely to monitor this gap; a utilization rate below roughly 65-75% usually signals pricing or staffing problems.

---

## Payment Processing Fees
URL: https://ratekit.org/glossary/payment-processing-fees
Payment processors like Stripe and PayPal charge a percentage plus a small fixed fee on every card transaction, which reduces what a seller actually receives from a sale.

Formula: Fee = (Amount × Percentage) + Fixed Fee

Every time a customer pays by card online, the payment processor — Stripe, PayPal, Square, and similar services — takes a cut before the money reaches the seller. The standard structure is a percentage of the transaction plus a small flat fee per transaction, commonly around 2.9% + $0.30 in the US for Stripe, slightly higher for PayPal's checkout product.

International cards, currency conversion, and manually-keyed transactions typically carry extra percentage points on top of the standard rate, which is why the same seller can see meaningfully different effective rates month to month depending on where their customers are paying from.

Sellers who want to pass the fee on to the customer, rather than absorb it, need to charge slightly more than the amount they actually want to receive — a flat percentage markup equal to the processor's rate isn't quite enough, because the fee is calculated on the higher, grossed-up charge amount.

---

## Cash Flow Forecast
URL: https://ratekit.org/glossary/cash-flow-forecast
A cash flow forecast projects how much cash a business will have on hand in future months, based on expected revenue, costs, and the starting cash balance.

Unlike a profit and loss statement, which can show a business as profitable "on paper" even when it's short on actual cash, a cash flow forecast tracks the thing that actually determines whether a business can pay its bills: the real cash balance in the bank, month by month.

A basic forecast starts with the current cash balance, then adds expected monthly revenue and subtracts expected monthly costs for each future period, carrying the running balance forward. More detailed forecasts build in multiple scenarios — what happens to the cash position if revenue comes in 25% below plan, or above it — since actual results rarely match the single most-likely projection exactly.

For a startup or any cash-constrained business, a 12-month rolling cash flow forecast is one of the most important documents to keep current, because it's what turns "runway" and "burn rate" from abstract concepts into an actual month where, if nothing changes, the business runs out of money.

---
